lesson.title: Straightening the Curve: The Arrhenius Plot
lesson.summary: Taking the natural log of both sides of the Arrhenius equation turns an exponential relationship into a straight line, giving chemists a genuinely practical way to measure a reaction's activation energy from real rate data.
lesson.body:
The Arrhenius equation, k = A e^(-Ea/RT), is exponential, and exponential relationships are awkward to work with directly: it is hard to look at a curved plot of k versus T and read off Ea by eye. Chemists solve this the same way they solve most exponential problems, by taking the natural log of both sides. Starting from k = A e^(-Ea/RT) and applying ln to both sides gives:

ln k = ln A - (Ea / R) * (1 / T)

Compare that to the equation of a straight line, y = m x + b. If you plot ln k on the y-axis against 1/T on the x-axis, you get a straight line whose slope m equals negative Ea over R, and whose y-intercept b equals ln A. This is the Arrhenius plot, and it is one of the most useful graphs in kinetics because it converts an experimental measurement problem (find Ea) into a graphing problem you already know how to solve: measure the rate constant k at several different temperatures, take the natural log of each k, take the reciprocal of each Kelvin temperature, plot the points, and read the slope off the best-fit line.

Let's work through the calculation with two data points, which is the simplest case and shows exactly how the slope translates into Ea. Suppose a reaction is measured at two temperatures: at T1 = 300 K, k1 = 3.0 x 10^-4 /s, and at T2 = 310 K, k2 = 6.0 x 10^-4 /s.

First take the natural logs: ln(3.0 x 10^-4) = -8.11, and ln(6.0 x 10^-4) = -7.42.

Next take the reciprocals of the temperatures: 1/T1 = 1/300 = 0.0033333 /K, and 1/T2 = 1/310 = 0.0032258 /K.

Now compute the slope, the change in ln k divided by the change in 1/T:

slope = (ln k2 - ln k1) / (1/T2 - 1/T1) = (-7.42 - (-8.11)) / (0.0032258 - 0.0033333) = 0.69 / (-0.0001075) = -6,450 K (approximately)

Since slope = -Ea / R, solve for Ea:

Ea = -slope * R = 6,450 K * 8.314 J/(mol K) = 53,600 J/mol = 53.6 kJ/mol

So this reaction has an activation energy of about 53.6 kJ/mol, extracted entirely from how much the rate constant changed between two temperatures. Notice something else about these numbers: the rate constant exactly doubled (from 3.0 x 10^-4 to 6.0 x 10^-4 /s) when the temperature rose by only 10 K, from 300 K to 310 K. That is not a coincidence tied to this specific example; it reflects the well-known rule of thumb that many ordinary reactions roughly double their rate for every 10 degree rise in temperature near room temperature, a pattern that corresponds to an activation energy somewhere in the range of about 50 to 60 kJ/mol. You will see this exact pair of temperatures and this exact doubling again in the Temperature and Rate chapter, where the same numbers get used to show why the rate constant is so much more sensitive to temperature than you might expect.

In real experiments, chemists rarely use just two points; they measure k at five, ten, or more temperatures and fit a line through all of them with linear regression, which averages out experimental noise and gives a more reliable slope. But the two-point version shown here captures the full logic: a straight Arrhenius plot is strong evidence that a reaction genuinely follows Arrhenius behavior, and its slope hands you Ea directly, no guessing required.
